text: Last lesson covered expectation value, the average outcome of a quantum measurement. This lesson covers the natural follow-up: how spread out are the actual outcomes around that average? Variance and standard deviation quantify that spread, and they're what tell you how many shots you actually need to trust an estimate.

Variance measures the average squared distance between a random variable's outcomes and its expectation value. Squaring matters — it makes every deviation positive, so opposite-direction distances don't cancel, and it penalizes large deviations more heavily. Standard deviation is simply the square root of variance, undoing that squaring step and converting back into the original units, so it reads as a typical distance from the mean.

Continuing the same example — P of 0 equal to 0.64, P of 1 equal to 0.36, outcomes plus and minus one, and an expectation value of 0.28 — the variance works out to 0.64 times 1 minus 0.28 squared, plus 0.36 times negative 1 minus 0.28 squared, which is 0.9216. Taking the square root gives a standard deviation of 0.96 — nearly as spread out as these two outcomes could possibly be, since 64-36 isn't that far from an even split.

If you're estimating an expectation value by averaging many repeated measurements, the uncertainty in that estimate shrinks as you take more shots — specifically, it scales as the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of shots. A higher-variance measurement genuinely needs more shots to pin down its expectation value to the same precision — a real, practical planning number for running quantum algorithms.
Next lesson reviews exactly the calculus you need for how quantum states evolve continuously over time: derivatives as rates of change, and what a differential equation actually is.
